# Hospital hygiene and trained nursing (`nursing_hospital_hygiene`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by hand_hygiene, sanitation_sewerage, data_graphs, contagion_theory
- Core idea: A hospital that crowds the sick together kills more than it cures unless it is run for cleanliness. One patient per bed with space between beds; windows that open; clean water and working drains; bedding and bandages boiled between patients; patients washed and fed properly; excrement and soiled dressings carried out and burnt or buried; fever, wound and childbirth cases in separate rooms with separate attendants. Nurses are trained, paid and sober, wash their hands between patients and keep written records. Count admissions and deaths by cause every month in the same way, so wards and hospitals can be compared and a change that works can be proved.
- Pitfalls:
  - Crediting kindness and scrubbing alone: deaths at Scutari fell only after the Sanitary Commission flushed the sewers and opened the ventilation in spring 1855
  - Explaining it by bad air; Nightingale herself did, and long doubted germs, yet the measures worked
  - Reusing one sponge, one basin and one probe from bed to bed
  - Building one huge hospital for all the sick of a city without separating fevers from wounds and births
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – legionary hospitals (valetudinaria) with separate small rooms; india: 3rd c. BC – Ashoka's edicts provide medical care for people and animals; 9th c. monastic hospital at Mihintale (Sri Lanka); islamic: 9th c. – bimaristans in Baghdad; 872 Ibn Tulun hospital, Cairo; 1284 Mansuri hospital, Cairo, with separate wards by disease, salaried staff and a pharmacy; europe: c. 370 – Basil's hospital at Caesarea; 1288 Santa Maria Nuova, Florence; 1788 Tenon exposes the Hôtel-Dieu in Paris with several patients per bed; 1854–1856 Nightingale at Scutari; 1860 nursing school at St Thomas's, London
- Read:
  - Florence Nightingale, Notes on Hospitals (3rd ed., 1863)
  - Florence Nightingale, Notes on Nursing: What It Is, and What It Is Not (1859)
  - Hugh Small, Florence Nightingale: Avenging Angel (1998)
